setting.unit_desc: Andean districts whose capitals lie within 50 km of the mita boundary in southern Peru; 4,038 individuals in the 2001 schooling sample, 179-183 districts in the census channel regressions

identification.variation: the mita conscription obligation changed discretely at the historical mita boundary; the study uses only the segment where elevation, ethnic distribution, 1573 tribute rates and demography are statistically identical across the boundary
identification.threat: RD validity requires all relevant factors besides treatment to vary smoothly at the boundary, and the multidimensional (longitude-latitude) discontinuity makes the choice of RD polynomial consequential

mechanisms.note: secure title for large landowners outside the mita raised returns to public goods; communal tenure in mita districts was abolished without enforceable peasant titling, inviting confiscation and rebell
the hacienda elite used political connections to obtain government funds and engineering for roads that persist today

settled: History affects contemporary economic outcomes, and extractive historical institutions lower long-run prosperity (Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson 2001, 2002; Nunn 2008; Glaeser & Shleifer 2002; Hall & Jo
Colonial policy restricted hacienda formation inside the mita catchment to limit competition for scarce mita labour, promoting communal tenure instead (Garrett 2005; Larson 1988)
contested: Whether historically high land inequality is the fundamental cause of Latin America's poor long-run growth (Engerman & Sokoloff 1997): here historical haciendas are positively associated with developm

Which channel carries historical persistence - property-rights enforcement, inequality, ethnic fractionalisation, barriers to entry or public goods - since existing aggregate evidence cannot distingui
gaps: General models of institutional evolution
How constraints on how the state can be used to shape economic interactions respond to forces promoting change
Whether the Peruvian masses would have been better off had initial land inequality been lower

setting.unit_desc: Brazilian municipalities with a mayor eligible for re-election; corruption levels of 376 municipalities had been audited and released before the October 2004 election

identification.variation: random selection of municipalities for audit plus the randomised timing of release before or after the 2004 election, compared at the same level of reported corruption
identification.threat: the auditing process itself could have differed systematically before and after the election (authors find no preferential treatment by party ties, political power or campaign contributions); and a municipality's corruption level and local-media availability are not exogenous, so they could proxy for other municipal characteristics

mechanisms.note: voters update priors and screen: corrupt incumbents are punished only once revealed corruption exceeds the median prior, and clean incumbents are rewarded (Besley 2005)
local radio presence is what converts the published report into votes, both exposing corrupt and promoting non-corrupt incumbents

settled: Accountability requires that voters have access to information allowing them to evaluate politician performance (Manin, Przeworski & Stokes 1999; Besley 2006)
A large theoretical literature agrees that better information to voters improves electoral accountability (Persson & Tabellini 2000; Besley & Prat 2006)
Information campaigns can reduce diversion of public funds: in Uganda schools' share of their entitlement rose 13% (Reinikka & Svensson 2005)
contested: Whether exposing corruption moves votes at all: earlier studies find only minor effects (Peters & Welch 1980 on the U.S. House; Chang & Golden 2004 on Italy)
Whether voters discount or ignore corruption information that can be politically manipulated and does not come from independent, reliable sources
Whether disclosure helps or hurts incumbents: the sign depends on voters' priors, so the average effect of the audits on re-election is insignificant
gaps: Whether public dissemination of audits upgrades the quality of the pool of politicians
Whether disclosure of audits actually reduces corruption
Whether disclosure of audits improves public policy

setting.unit_desc: audited municipalities with population under 450,000 (the anti-corruption programme's universe is 5,118 such municipalities, which received R$24.8 billion of transfers in 2002); mayors serving the 2001-2004 term

identification.variation: term limits: a comparison of first- versus second-term mayors using variation only within audit lottery and state, with a full set of mayor and municipal controls; corroborated by an RD on municipalities where the 2000 incumbent barely won or barely lost
identification.threat: no experimental variation in term status, so the comparison must assume selection on observables; unobserved differences in municipal characteristics, mayoral political ability, and learning-by-doing in office could drive the gap, and rational voters may select less corrupt politicians into lame-duck terms

mechanisms.note: the discipline effect dominates: mayors who can still be re-elected extract fewer rents, as in Barro-Ferejohn agency models
positive selection into lame-duck terms works against the discipline effect, but second-term mayors are still more corrupt than first-termers who are later re-elected
term-limited mayors who later seek higher office are 4.9pp less corrupt than other second-term mayors
electoral discipline substitutes for information and judicial threat: with local radio or a local prosecutor there is little first/second-term differential

settled: The pervasive effects of corruption on economic development are well documented, while its root causes are poorly understood (Knack & Keefer 1995; Mauro 1995; Bertrand et al. 2007)
Political agency models predict incumbents refrain from maximum rent extraction in their first term to secure re-election and future rents (Barro 1970; Ferejohn 1986; Banks & Sundaram 1993)
Voters punish corrupt politicians when information about corruption is publicised (Ferraz & Finan 2008)
contested: Whether specific electoral structures discipline politicians' behaviour, since most evidence uses perception indices rather than measured corruption

Cross-country evidence linking electoral rules to corruption is hard to interpret because the full set of institutional arrangements determining corruption cannot be held fixed (Adsera, Boix & Payne 2
Whether term limits raise or lower rent extraction, because the discipline effect and the positive selection of less corrupt types into lame-duck terms pull in opposite directions (Besley 2006; Smart
gaps: Whether electoral accountability affects aspects of governance other than corruption
Whether electoral accountability ultimately improves voters' welfare

C00170.claim: The Great Plains buffalo slaughter was triggered by a European tanning innovation and sustained by foreign demand for hides, acting through very elastic demand and open access to hunting rather than the usual suspects.
C00170.treatment_desc: tanning innovation making buffalo hides valuable industrial leather, with fixed world prices and European demand
C00170.outcome_desc: buffalo kill, hunter entry and herd size on the Great Plains

setting.unit_desc: Great Plains buffalo herd; hide export and import-share statistics from several countries

identification.variation: timing of the tanning innovation and US-specific shares of European hide imports, combined with a dynamic open-access model and first-person accounts
identification.threat: evidence is largely circumstantial

settled: Hide hunting, the US Army, native overhunting and the railroads are typically held responsible for the slaughter
contested: Whether international trade, rather than the usual suspects, drove the slaughter (role of trade featured minimally in prior accounts)
gaps: The Canadian case of bison extinction is left for future work
C00170.data_asset: constructed hide export data from international trade statistics, plus diaries and newspaper accounts
C00170.scope: explains the punctuated slaughter on the plains after 1872; requires very elastic demand, open access and a new tanning process jointly

C01422.claim: When the strong party controls a source of unrest, it wins more often the less is known about its ability to cause unrest, because a better-informed weak party can moderate to a centrist platform; uncertainty over the threat's credibility leads to platform div
C01422.treatment_desc: a party able to instigate political unrest (riots, strikes, coups) if it loses the election (model)
C01422.outcome_desc: platform choice, which party wins, and implemented policy

setting.unit_desc: theoretical two-party majority-rule election with a one-dimensional policy space; illustrated with UK, Taiwan, El Salvador and Liberia

identification.variation: model comparing platform commitment vs. none, and public vs. private information about the strong party's ability to cause unrest

mechanisms.note: the strong party becomes more likely to win as voter fear of disruption grows when the risk of unrest is its private information
signalling by the strong party under private information produces platform divergence
platform convergence arises with commitment and no private information, but the strong party wins on the convergent policy if it controls a serious threat

gaps: Elections with more than two parties or more than one threatening actor (model has two parties and a single threatening actor; the convergence theorem fails with more than two parties, Shepsle 1991)
C01422.scope: results depend on whether the threat is controlled by the strong party or by an outsider, and on whether risk is privately known; robust to large benefits of office only when an outsider controls the threat
